newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Anglo seen poised for giant Brazil footing.
newsitem.headline: Anglo seen poised for giant Brazil footing.

text.p: Anglo American Corp of South Africa is set to win a footing in Brazil's state mining giant CVRD, lining up control of the world's biggest pulp and iron ore interests as a future prize, analysts said on Wednesday.

Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) is the world's largest iron ore producer and has significant pulp and paper interests in Brazil. A 45 percent stake in CVRD is due to be auctioned later on Wednesday despite mass protests to try and halt the privatisation sale.

Anglo and Brazil's largest conglomerate, pulp, cement and metal concern Votorantim Celulose E Papel SA, lead the Valecom consortium bidding for the stake. Together Anglo and Votorantim control 50 percent of the consortium.
Analysts say that Anglo's bid is likely to succeed because it will offer the best price to secure a long-term future.
Winning the CVRD bid would give the South African mining house a rapid and focused international footing, denied it under economic sanctions during the apartheid isolation years.

"Anglo's biggest problem is that it has been trapped by national boundaries. This is a one-off deal that allows them to get a lot of their focus offshore," said Trevor Pearton, head of mining research at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
"Anglo will probably pay too much for it. They're a longer-term player and they want control in the long-term. It will position them very strongly in another country," he said.
But the analysts said this could lead to a re-evaluation of the corporate profile of both Anglo and its historical offshore arm Minorco SA which itself has interests in Brazil.
"This might be the ideal time to restructure. There are enormous opportunities coming out of this, but what does Anglo want to be," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
South Africa's foreign exchange controls are hampering a realignment of Anglo and Minorco, Pearton said.

CVRD owns the world's largest iron ore deposits. Its Carajas mine in the Amazon is thought to hold 18 billion metric tonnes. "This (winning the bid) could catapult Minorco/Anglo into the role of the world's biggest iron ore producer," said Barry Sergeant, mining financials analyst at BOE Natwest.

Amongst other pulp and paper interests in Brazil -- the world's lowest-cost pulp producer -- CVRD also owns 42.5 percent of the country's second biggest pulp maker Celmar Industria de Celulose Papel which is due to start production in 2001 with 500,000 tonnes per annum.

Anglo's wholly-owned subsidiary Mondi Brazil Ltd owns 28 percent of the voting capital or 11.8 percent of the equity of Brazil's Aracruz Celulose, the world's largest producer of bleached hardwood kraft market pulp.
Through its Anglo American Industrial Corp Ltd (Amic), Anglo also has significant pulp and paper interests in South Africa, Europe and the U.S.
"At the end of the day, assuming the (CVRD) bid is successful, this could make Anglo/Minorco one of the largest pulp producers in the world," Sergeant said.

"CVRD has deliberately grown its paper interests in Brazil. There is a very good chance that there could be a consolidation between CVRD and Aracruz's pulp interests. Minorco has put an enormous effort into expanding Minorco paper," he added.

The privatization of CVRD should raise at least $5 billion once completed and would be the biggest Latin American state sell-off ever. Besides the Anglo/Votorantim consortium, a group led by Brazilian steelmaker CSN is also bidding.
The National Development Bank (BNDES) said the CVRD auction was officially suspended until 1300 GMT on Wednesday.
In the wake of riots involving leftist protesters against the privatisation, Brazil's government lodged an appeal on Tuesday with a high court to keep the sell-off on track.
